sources.claim: Outright International's Philippines country overview (updated 12 March 2026): same-sex conduct legal nationwide; no legal gender recognition (still required: no LGR pathway); Executive Order 100 s.2019 (signed 17 Dec 2019) created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, amended by EO 51 s.2023 to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee, neither implemented as of 2025; anti-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels but national legislation filed since 1999 has not been enacted; a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in the Philippines - Wikipedia
sources.claim: National framework page (applies to Davao Region, which records no separate regional legislation; the national position plus any local ordinance of Davao City, the region's administrative center, is what a visitor stands under). Same-sex sexual activity is legal in the Philippines, but there is no national anti-discrimination statute - protection runs only in the basic-education context, with many local government non-discrimination ordinances filling the gap - and transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender. Same-sex marriage and civil unions have no national recognition, the Family Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has been repeatedly filed without enactment. The page's local-government-ordinances section lists Davao City (2012) among the localities with a non-discrimination ordinance, giving this region a dated, on-jurisdiction datapoint.

sources.title: Davao council bans discrimination vs gays, minority, differently abled - INQUIRER.net
sources.claim: INQUIRER.net (14 Dec 2012) reported that the Davao City council passed an ordinance banning discrimination against gays (LGBT people), minorities and differently-abled persons - a direct, dated report of the 2012 Davao City non-discrimination ordinance that the national LGBTQ-rights page cites as its Davao (2012) entry. Genuinely on-jurisdiction for Davao Region, whose administrative center is Davao City.

records.name: Caraga
records.current_summary:
Caraga has no documented region-specific laws affecting transgender people; the national framework is what applies here: same-sex conduct is legal, there is no legal gender-recognition pathway, national SOGIE equality legislation has been filed since 1999 without enactment, and anti-discrimination ordinances exist only at some city and provincial levels. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs, school anti-bullying rules and gender-responsive education policy cover SOGI grounds, and executive orders created a national diversity-and-inclusion programme that, per audited reporting, remained unimplemented as of 2025.

Acceptance runs partial: a 2018 national survey recorded about one-fifth support for same-sex civil unions and majority opposition to trans women's use of women's toilets. A June 2025 report on the killing of an eighteen-year-old trans student, which a national alliance presented as part of a pattern of violence against trans Filipinas, originates in a different region — it is Caraga only as part of the archipelago-wide climate, and is recorded as exactly that.

sources.claim: Chile country dossier (Outright International, published March 12, 2026) contains no Antofagasta-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding, which is the basis for this record's national-score assessment: same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; the hate-crime law has covered sexual orientation and gender identity since 2012; legal gender recognition by self-determination since 2019; a third sex option on birth certificates since 2006; and the 2025-26 rollback in which the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children. The dossier itself carries no division-specific information.

Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) supplies this record's division-specific figures from its national regional table: Antofagasta is placed at 2.09% of nationally documented abuse cases, with a +45.45% year-on-year rise in 2025, the second-largest regional increase after La Araucania (+150%). Nationally, the report records a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025 (+27.1%, the highest in 24 years), with only Valparaiso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) falling while the other 14 regions rose; it reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate, which is what this record's mid-share reading rests on. The 2024 share cited in this record's comparison is not reproduced in this 2025 edition.

records.name: Gangwon
records.current_summary:
No province-specific law, ordinance or enforcement pattern targeting trans people is documented for Gangwon; the framework a visitor meets there is the national one: being trans is not criminalised, and the courts are steadily tightening what legal gender recognition may demand — a May 2024 ruling ended any surgical requirement for changing registered sex, and in July 2024 a court held that police telling a trans person to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed their rights, awarding damages after both instances found for the claimant and an appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.

The same sources describe both the promise and the limit of that judicial route: a 2021 damages award against an academy that barred a trans student from restrooms shows recourse exists, while a 2021 national survey of 591 trans respondents — 41% using wrong-gender facilities out of fear, 39% restricting food and drink to avoid restrooms, 36% skipping facilities altogether — shows everyday facility avoidance remains the norm. For a visitor, Gangwon's audited record offers legality, functioning courts and no local hostility machinery, with social friction around public restrooms documented nationally rather than locally.

sources.claim: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award (against a 3 million won claim), ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female - who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 - to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The article also reports a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents (41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink, 36% forwent restroom use) and a 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. This is the national framework this province is scored against; no KOR/Gangwon-specific incident appears.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now only reference, not criteria; the court said every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the framework this province is scored against; the wire contains no KOR/Gangwon-specific content.

records.name: Incheon
records.current_summary:
Incheon is documented by the audited record as a place with no specific local laws, ordinances or incident patterns concerning trans people; visitors stand under the national framework, which is favourable on paper and improving through litigation: trans status is not a crime; a May 2024 ruling confirmed surgery cannot be required to change registered legal sex; and in July 2024 a court held that police directing a transitioning person to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, an appellate court branding comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.

The same record supplies the practical counterweight: a 2021 national survey of trans respondents documents fear-driven restroom avoidance in striking majorities (41% had used a facility mismatching their identity; 36% forwent restroom use), and a 2021 award against a private academy that excluded a trans student shows courts intervene when facilities are denied. That mix — lawful status, an active and increasingly sympathetic judiciary, and socially contested facilities — is the documented experience of Incheon, no municipality-level initiative here being recorded either way.
